newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Australia rate cut likely by year end - Westpac.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Australia rate cut likely by year end - Westpac.

text.p: Westpac Banking Corp Ltd said on Thursday there was a 75 percent probability that Australian official interest rates would be cut by the end of the year.
"It's safer to have an interest rate cut now than it was in 1993," said Bill Evans, Westpac's General Manager Economics.
Evans said the main factors were the weak labour market, the government's tough fiscal stance and the relative strength of the Australian dollar.
However, Evans saw the Australian dollar falling to US$0.7700 by the end of the year as it lost support from Japanese demand for dual currency samurai bonds.

Westpac economists see the prospect of a further local easing in policy making Australia's yield advantage at the short-end of the curve over the U.S. less attractive for Japanese investors through the samurai market.
They see this spread contracting to further to around 40 basis points from a current level of 70 basis points.
The Australian unit has benefitted for demand for this form of samuari bond when support from commodity prices has waned.
But the weakness in the currency should be short-lived with commodities rebounding next year and Westpac sees the exchange rate at US$0.80 in the first half of 1997 and $0.82 by year-end.

Announcing two new monthly publications -- the Westpac Australian Interest Rate Report and Currency Report -- the bank said over a three month horizon it put odds on a 75 percent for an easing; 25 percent for no change and nil for a tightening.
Westpac sees a 50 basis point cut mostly likely in November to 6.50 percent, and then holding steady until the first half of 1998 when it sees it back up to 7.25 percent.

It said the relatively clear domestic picture for fixed interest markets is clouded by the monetary policy uncertainty in the U.S. and is factoring in post-election rate rises which will cause some tumult in financial markets.

"(But) in the short term at least stronger domestic inflation and fiscal fundamentals and the domestic bias towards easing will allow domestic bonds to ride this coming storm out relatively well," the bank said in a summary of the report.
Also surveying foreign fixed interest rate managers, Westpac found offshore fund managers expected a further yield spread compression against U.S. Treasuries.
Many U.S. managers noted that a 100 basis point spread is their key target by year-end compared with 123 basis points at the time of the survey.
